title: Comfort, lived
hookLine: the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av, "Comfort ye", begins seven weeks of comfort
tomorrow: who decides what goes on your calendar?

cards: When someone you love is grieving, the hardest part is often the first sentence. Everything you version sounds wrong. So what does the prophet say first, on the Shabbat after the floor?

Two words, and then the same two again: "Comfort ye, comfort ye My people, saith your God." That Shabbat is called Shabbat Nachamu, the Shabbat of comfort, after the first word of its reading from Isaiah.
And the comfort doesn't stop after one week.

teach.h: A DAY OF SORROW, A SEASON OF COMFORT.
teach.b: After Tisha B'Av come seven Shabbatot of comfort readings from Isaiah, leading toward Rosh Hashanah. The sorrow gets a day; the comfort gets a season.
And notice the doubling: comfort ye, comfort ye. Some readers hear comfort that has to be said more than once, because grief doesn't hear it the first time.
The tradition also teaches how to comfort one person, not only a people.
When Job's friends hear of his losses, they come and sit with him on the ground, and the text says "none spoke a word unto him; for they saw that his grief was very great."

teach.h: SIT DOWN. LET THEM SPEAK FIRST.
teach.b: The Talmud draws a rule from visits like that: those who come to comfort a mourner don't speak until the mourner speaks first. Comfort starts as presence. Words come second, and they follow the grieving person's lead.
When visitors leave a house of mourning, there's a traditional line for the mourner: may God comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem.
The private loss is held inside a larger one, also waiting for comfort. So comfort, lived, is small: show up, sit down, let them speak first, and keep coming back for weeks, not only the first day.

how: On the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av, synagogues read Isaiah 40, 'Comfort ye', the first of the comfort readings that continue until Rosh Hashanah; visitors to a house of mourning sit quietly, let the mourner speak first, and leave with a traditional line of comfort.

games.q: your coworker's father died. you visit, and she's staring at the coffee table, saying nothing. what's the move?
o: sit down and wait; let her speak first.
fill the quiet with your own story of a loss.
give her a list of things that helped you.
games.why: the Talmud: comforters don't speak until the mourner does. Job's friends began well: they sat on the ground and said nothing.

practice: Bring to mind one person carrying something heavy right now. Write a short text you could send them, just a few words, with no advice in it at all: only that you're thinking of them, or that you're there.
Read it once, slowly, and decide when it should go.

wordCard.voice: Shabbat Nachamu: the Shabbat of comfort after Tisha B'Av, named for Isaiah's first words, comfort ye, comfort ye.

orig.note: Hebrew: comfort (said to many); the first word of Isaiah 40, said twice.

carryVoice: A line to carry: comfort follows, slowly, and it usually starts by sitting down. Until next time.
